events.before: Home Newsroom JLCCNC Participates in Hannover Messe 2025 JLCCNC Participates in Hannover Messe 2025 Press Release Mar 10, 2025 JLCCNC will exhibit at Hannover Messe from 31 March to 4 April 2025 at Hannover Messe in Germany. With the theme of ‘Energising A Sustainable Industry’, JLC Global will be showcasing its full range of technologies in 3D printing, CNC machining, Mechanical Components, PCB, PCBA and PCB design software development in Hall 17, Booth B12, demonstrating its expertise in smart manufacturing and digital transformation. It demonstrates its leading strength in the field of intelligent manufacturing and digital transformation. Exhibition Information · Event Theme : Hannover Messe 2025 - "Energizing A Sustainable Industry" · Dates : March 31 to April 4, 2025 · Location : Hannover Exhibition Center, 30521 Hannover, Germany · JLCCNC Booth : Hall 17, Stand B12 (together with JLCPCB) · Exhibits : 3D Printing, CNC Machining, Mechanical Components , PCB, PCBA, PCB Design Software Development 1. Exhibition Background As one of the world's largest and most influential industrial events, Hannover Messe has always been the wind vane for global industrial automation, digital manufacturing and sustainable industrial development. With the theme of ‘Energising A Sustainable Industry’, this year's fair focuses on green energy, intelligent manufacturing and sustainable development, and attracts many global leading enterprises and experts to gather and discuss the new trends of future industry. 2. About JLC Global JLC Global is a comprehensive technology company dedicated to promoting industrial intelligence and digital transformation. The company focuses on the R&D and production of 3D printing, CNC machining, automated production, and the whole industry chain of electronic manufacturing such as PCB and PCBA. Relying on strong technological strength and innovative R&D capabilities, JLC Global continues to provide efficient and accurate manufacturing solutions for global customers and leads the industry with continuous technological innovation. In recent years, JLC Global has made remarkable achievements in the field of intelligent manufacturing and green production, and has successfully implemented a number of major projects to create a sustainable and efficient production system for its customers. 3. Exhibition Highlights and Product/Technology Details In this Hannover Messe, JLC Global will comprehensively display the core technologies and innovative products of its entire business line, specifically including: CNC Machining : The company will display advanced CNC machining systems to ensure efficient and accurate parts machining capability. 3D Printing : Showcasing high-precision, rapid prototyping 3D printing technology to meet diversified industrial manufacturing needs. Mechanical Components : JLC Mechatronic Components Marketplace integrates various mechatronic parts, aiming to provide a one-stop service for factory automation. PCB & PCBA : Showcasing the whole industry chain services from PCB design, manufacturing to assembly, helping the rapid iteration of electronic products. PCB Design Software Development : Introducing self-developed PCB design software to enhance design efficiency and product innovation. At the exhibition site, visitors will have the opportunity to fully understand JLC Global's innovations in process, technology and products, and deeply experience the company's all-round solutions in the field of intelligent manufacturing through interactive experience. 4. More Information For more exhibition activities and the latest news of JLCCNC, please visit our official website and follow our official social media platforms. We will be arranging on-site experts to answer questions and provide technical demonstrations, and we sincerely invite all professionals to come and exchange views, and witness the future changes of industrial technology together. If you have CNC machining needs, click to get a free quote for our cnc machining services. events.before: Home Newsroom JLCCNC Announces Website Upgrade and Improved Mobile Experience JLCCNC Announces Website Upgrade and Improved Mobile Experience Press Release Dec 27, 2025 Table of Contents About JLCCNC Media Contact: December 27, 2025 — JLCCNC announced the completion of a website visual and functional upgrade, aimed at improving content clarity, navigation efficiency, and overall user experience across devices. This update reflects JLCCNC’s ongoing commitment to providing a clearer and more accessible platform for engineers, designers, and manufacturing professionals worldwide. As part of this upgrade, JLCCNC has optimized the structure and usability of several core informational sections, including: ● About Us ● Coupons ● Help Center ● News ● Blog In addition, all existing product and service pages, including CNC machining and Sheet Metal pages, have been updated to improve content clarity and usability. JLCCNC has also added a new Customer Reviews & Testimonials page, enabling users to view real project experiences and feedback. Furthermore, all manufacturing process introduction pages have been comprehensively enhanced with clearer and more structured content, with a stronger focus on: ● Design guidelines ● Manufacturing workflows These improvements help users better understand JLCCNC’s machining and sheet metal capabilities during the design and quotation stages, enabling more informed manufacturing decisions. To further enhance accessibility, the website has been fully optimized for mobile devices, providing smoother navigation, improved readability, and a more consistent browsing experience across screens. JLCCNC welcomes user feedback and suggestions as part of its continuous platform improvement efforts. About JLCCNC JLCCNC is a professional CNC and Sheet Metal service provider, offering high-precision milling, turning, and sheet metal fabrication with fast turnaround times and reliable manufacturing quality for customers worldwide. events.before: Home Newsroom 2026 June Holiday Schedule 2026 June Holiday Schedule Press Release Jun 13, 2026 Table of Contents Production & Delivery Notes: JLCCNC Factories Holiday Schedule Logistics Companies Schedule Customer Support Schedule [ June 13, 2026 ] – JLCCNC today released its June holiday schedule. Please be informed that due to the holiday, JLCCNC will adjust its operation and production schedules from June 19th to June 21st, 2026 . While our online platform remains fully operational, factory production capacities and shipping schedules will be partially affected during this period. Production & Delivery Notes: ● Ordering: Normal. You can place quotes and orders at any time as usual. ● Production: Suspended. Factory production lines will be paused on June 19th for most factories. The CNC factory will be paused on June 19th and June 21st . ● Shipping: Delayed. Regular dispatch will be suspended during the holiday and will resume progressively on June 22nd, 2026 . ● Lead Time: Postponed. The estimated lead time for all orders affected by the holiday will be extended by 1-3 days accordingly. JLCCNC Factories Holiday Schedule Logistics Companies Schedule Note：No impact on the In-stock Parts Service; in-stock parts are added to your library immediately after checkout. Customer Support Schedule Email and Livechat support will remain available on June 19th and June 20th, and will be suspended on June 21st. Warm Tip: To avoid any project delays caused by the holiday production pause and potential logistics bottlenecks, we highly recommend planning your schedule ahead and placing orders early. Thank you for your understanding and continuous support! events.before: Home Newsroom Keep Production on Lunar New Year Holiday 2025 Keep Production on Lunar New Year Holiday 2025 Press Release Jan 13, 2025 The Lunar New Year is approaching, and we are so grateful for your support over the past year. The Lunar New Year holiday will span from January 23rd to February 4th . All CNC Machining materials will continue production during the LNY holiday, except for Steel 45#, SUS304. Spray Painting service is unavailable . Note: The build time might be 2-3 days longer than usual during the LNY holiday. During the Lunar New Year holiday, 3D printing and CNC machining orders cannot be combined for shipping, nor can they be combined with PCB/Stencil orders. This will resume on February 5th. Below is the production and shipping schedule. Please kindly schedule the order placement time properly to guarantee the timely completion of your projects. Factory & Shipping Schedule: Order Schedule for reference: Notes: · There is no shipping pickup service on Sunday, January 19th. · The 'Confirm Date' is the day when your order's manufacturing data is complete and the order is prepared for production. If you have any questions about the above information or need order support, please contact our customer service team support@jlcpcb.com . events.before: Home Newsroom Service Availability during the Annual Spring Festival Service Availability during the Annual Spring Festival Press Release Jan 27, 2026 Table of Contents Available Services During Spring Festival Holiday Order Placement Notes The Spring Festival (Lunar New Year) is approaching, and we are so grateful for your support over the past year. The Spring Festival holiday will span from February 10 to February 23 . JLC will continue to support your manufacturing needs during the Spring Festival holiday. We will provide the same high-quality manufacturing services for PCB, PCBA, 3D Printing, CNC machining, and mechatronic parts sourcing , and more . Below are the available services during the holiday, along with the production and shipping schedule. We recommend scheduling order placement in advance to help ensure timely project completion. Production & Shipping Schedule: Order Placement Schedule (For Reference): Available Services During Spring Festival Holiday CNC Machining All CNC machining materials will remain in production during the Spring Festival holiday, except for Steel 45# and SUS304 . Spray painting , mirror polishing , transparent polishing and blue-tinted transparent polishing services will be unavailable. Please note the following limitations during the holiday period: · The maximum supported part size is 500 × 500 × 200 mm . · Parts with highly complex structures requiring 5-axis machining are not supported. Note: Build times may be extended by 2–3 days during the Spring Festival holiday. Sheet Metal Sheet Metal Service is unavailable from February 10 to February 23. Orders placed during the Spring Festival holiday will be processed starting from February 24. PCB & PCBA Services Notes: Build times may be extended by around 2 days during the Spring Festival holiday. SMT-Stencil Service SMT-stencil orders will remain in production during the Spring Festival holiday. SMT-stencil build time: 3 days Parts Orders Types Production Availability JLCPCB In-stock Parts No impact on order processing. JLCPCB Pre-order Parts Unavailable from February 15 to February 23. Global Sourcing Parts Unavailable from February 15 to February 23. Consigned Parts Service(ship from outside Mainland China) Unavailable from February 15 to February 23. Consigned Parts Service(ship from Mainland China) No impact on order processing. Flexible Heater Flexible Heater Service is unavailable from February 10 to February 23. Orders placed during the Spring Festival holiday will be processed starting from February 24 . PCB Layout PCB Layout Service is unavailable from February 10 to February 23. Orders placed during the Spring Festival holiday will be processed starting from February 24 . 3D Printing All 3D printing materials will remain in production during the Spring Festival holiday, except for the BJ-316L material. Note: Build times may be extended by 2–3 days during the Spring Festival holiday. JLCMC- Mechatronic Parts Service Types Shipping Availability In-stock Parts Can be shipped during the Spring Festival holiday, except February 16 to February 19. Back-orders Parts Service is unavailable from February 10 to February 23. Orders placed during the Spring Festival holiday will be processed starting from February 24. API Application (JLCAPI.com) The API applications submitted between February 10 and February 24 will be reviewed on February 24, 2026. Order Placement Notes 1. Orders scheduled for production from February 2 to February 23 cannot be combined with orders scheduled for production after the holiday. 2. During the Spring Festival holiday, the order combining rules are as follows: · PCB / PCBA / Stencil: Can be combined and shipped together, but cannot be combined with other product types. · 3D Printing, CNC Machining, Sheet Metal, Flexible Heater, Mechatronic Parts: Must be ordered separately. 3. Except for New User Coupons and after-sales compensation coupons, all other coupons will be temporarily unavailable during the Spring Festival holiday, and their validity periods will be extended accordingly. 4. JLC Balance Top-up and Withdrawal Schedule · Top-up: Suspended from February 17 to February 19 · Withdrawal: Suspended from February 10 to February 23 5. Verify Now Blog > Electrical Discharge Machining (EDM) Design Guidelines Electrical Discharge Machining (EDM) Design Guidelines by: Mila Sep 01,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in CNC Machining electrical discharge machining Wire EDM cnc edm cnc wire edm cnc wire cut This guideline provides DFM (Design for Manufacturability) specifications for EDM for structural and mechanical designers. It helps prevent common issues including excessive spark‑off corner radius, poor flushing‑caused defects, dimension deviation from electrode wear, recast‑layer fatigue cracks and out‑of‑tolerance dimensions during design‑and‑drawing stages. （EDM Working Principle） 1. Manufacturing Limits & Tolerance Specifications At the early design phase, verify that part dimensions and tolerances match EDM machine capability boundaries. Minimum Manufacturable Feature Size: Down to 0.05 mm (highly dependent on electrode diameter and geometry). Maximum Workpiece Dimensions: Limited by machine envelope, up to 800 x 600 mm travel range. Internal Corner Limitations: 0.025 mm ~ 0.10 mm. Determined by different wire-cut processes. Thickness & Accuracy Correlation: Thickness from 0.05 mm ~ 1.0 mm；Dimensional tolerance from ±0.002 mm ~ ±0.02 mm. Determined by different wire-cut processes. 2. Major Types of EDM Processes Based on kinematics, electrode configuration, and target industrial applications, non-traditional electro-discharge manufacturing is categorized into four primary configurations: Wire EDM (Wire-Cut Electrical Discharge Machining) In a standard Wire EDM setup, a continuously traveling thin brass or coated wire (typically 0.1–0.3 mm in diameter) serves as the cutting electrode tool. Guided by computerized numerical control, high-precision trajectory planning and continuous wire feeding ensure high processing stability. Under optimal machine calibration, material selection, and parameters, modern cnc wire cut technology can easily achieve sub-micron dimensional control. Parts processed via cnc wire cut exhibit virtually no mechanical burrs common in conventional milling, although minor spark erosion tracks and a thin recast layer remain. This process is extensively applied to complex 2D profiles, narrow slots, irregular keyways, and tapered precision geometries. Sinker EDM (Ram / Die-Sinking EDM) Sinker EDM utilizes custom-machined 3D copper or graphite electrodes. Controlled spark erosion between the shaped electrode and workpiece gradually replicates the exact inverted form onto the part. This method excels at forming blind cavities and intricate concave structures. Because electrode wear occurs dynamically during operation, precise multi-stage tool switching is essential. Sinker units often incorporate advanced cnc edm controllers to compensate for wear paths, serving as a pillar process in injection mold, die casting, and stamping tool production. Hole Drilling EDM (Fast Hole Spark Drilling) Hole drilling EDM uses a tubular rotating electrode combined with internal high-pressure dielectric flushing to clear erosion debris. It specializes in drilling tiny deep holes or angled channels into hard metals such as cemented carbide and nickel superalloys. Widely used for turbine blade cooling holes and fuel nozzle micro-apertures, it eliminates traditional drill bit breakage issues. Additionally, high-speed hole drillers are regularly deployed to produce starting pilot holes for subsequent cnc wire edm cutting operations. Micro EDM Micro EDM utilizes ultra-fine electrodes and extremely small pulse discharge energy to produce micro-scale features down to a few micrometers. By minimizing single-discharge energy, the thermal affect zone (HAZ) is significantly reduced, making it ideal for medical implants, micro-fluidic channels, and micro-electronic components. 3. Key Advantages of Electrical Discharge Machining Machining Super-Hard Conductive Materials: Material hardness imposes almost no barrier. High-hardness alloys like quenched tool steels, tungsten carbide, titanium alloys, and Inconel can be machined easily. Ultra-High Precision Capability: Under controlled environment and parameters, electro-discharge equipment delivers micron-level dimensional accuracy across complex features. Near-Zero Mechanical Cutting Forces: Because physical tool-to-workpiece contact is avoided, mechanical cutting force is virtually non-existent, eliminating physical deformation risks on ultra-thin walls. Extreme Geometric Versatility: Capable of producing sharp internal corners, deep narrow cavities, micro-slots, and high aspect-ratio holes impossible for rotative cutters. Superior Surface Finish Potential: Multi-pass fine-finishing cycles yield extremely low surface roughness without directional tool marks, despite microscopic discharge pit textures. 4. Process Limitations & Design Considerations Internal Corner Radius Rule: Minimum internal corner radius for wire-cut EDM is approximately equal to the wire radius + discharge gap. Theoretical zero-radius sharp internal corners cannot be manufactured and should not be specified on drawings. Engineering Example: Using a 0.2 mm diameter wire typically results in a minimum internal corner radius of ≥ 0.13 mm. Slot / Gap Aspect Ratio Rule : Avoid excessive depth-to-width ratios for narrow slots. An aspect ratio exceeding 20:1 severely restricts dielectric flushing, leading to secondary discharge, degraded dimensional accuracy, and exponential increases in machining time. Sinker‑EDM Cavity Depth Rule: Electrode wear increases progressively with cavity depth in sinker EDM. Dimensional wear compensation allowance is required for deep features. Recommendation: For deep cavities, pre-machining (e.g., rough milling via CNC) to remove bulk stock prior to EDM finishing is highly recommended to reduce electrode wear and cycle time. Micro‑hole Drilling EDM Rule : For blind micro-holes, dimensional stability and taper control decrease as hole depth increases. Through-hole EDM drilling provides significantly more stable accuracy and better flushing condition than blind holes. 5. Electrical Discharge Machining vs. Traditional CNC Machining Traditional CNC milling relies on solid cutting tools to mechanically shear metal chips. Mechanical tool wear is present, internal sharp corners are limited by tool radii, and thin-walled parts risk mechanical deflection. In contrast, cnc edm relies on thermal spark erosion without physical cutter contact pressure. In modern toolrooms, these technologies are complementary rather than competing: heavy material removal and outer profiles are first handled by high-efficiency CNC milling, after which precision features are finished using a high-precision cnc wire edm unit or sinker machine. 6. File Preparation Requirements(CAD/DFM) 2D DXF/DWG Files Maintain 1:1 scale. Remove duplicate lines, construction geometry and open contours. Draw target dimensions directly; do not manually compensate discharge gaps — leave gap compensation to manufacturing engineers. 3D STEP/STP/IGES Models Export complete solid‑part geometry. Do not embed electrode solids inside models. Cloud‑manufacturing‑platform DFM algorithms will identify part features automatically. Engineering Drawings Clearly mark tolerance requirements, recast‑layer‑removal requirements, Ra surface roughness, and whether holes are through‑holes or blind holes. 7. EDM Design Checklist Confirm that the part material is electrically conductive Provide reasonable discharge fillets at internal corners; do not design with theoretical sharp corners Ensure that the depth-to-width ratio of slits/deep grooves is within the process tolerance limits Clearly specify the removal of the EDM remelted layer for high-fatigue applications Prioritize CNC rough machining for deep cavities to reduce the material removal volume required for EDM Ensure dimensional tolerances match the actual capabilities of EDM; do not set tolerances that exceed process limits Ensure dimensions are completely consistent across drawings, DXF, and STEP files Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > PCBWay Plug-In for FreeCAD PCBWay Plug-In for FreeCAD by: Anson Jul 29,2022 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in CNC Machining FreeCAD CNC machining 3D printing Sheet metal Injection molding Send your 3D design to PCBWay for instant production with just one click. PCBWay's 3D & CNC services always well received by our customers. Now we have an in-depth cooperation with FreeCAD. FreeCAD is an open-source parametric 3D modeler made primarily to design real-life objects of any size. It is widely used among engineers. Now when you complete the 3D design on FreeCAD, you can place an order on PCBWay with just one click. FreeCAD will pass step files to us. You can click "Save to Cart" to place an order immediately after uploading the files (usually only takes a few seconds), our engineers will double check the files before production. Installation from the official FreeCAD tools Just click the "tools" ----“Addon manager”---Choose the "PCBWay” from the selection list, click and install it. Manual installation You can also download the latest file from https://github.com/pcbway/PCBWay-Plug-in-for-FreeCAD , then click the "Macro", put the python file in the path, and click the “execute“ As a sponsor of FreeCAD, we will always support its development. Note: Thanks to the open source community. Any feedback or questions please contact with anson@pcbway.com Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > PCBWay Fabrication Toolkit for Kicad PCBWay Fabrication Toolkit for Kicad by: PCBWay Oct 11,2023 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in News Recently, PCBWay added a plug-in called PCBWay Fabrication Toolkit to Kicad: With just one click of the mouse, four files can be exported from the layout file automatically: Gerber file, IPC-Netlist file, BOM file and Pick and Place file, which can significantly improves the efficiency of pre-production work. Installation from the Official KiCad Repositories After installation, the plugin will appear on the right side of the navigation bar. And users can use it to export all the production files with just a click. Process demonstration： Sending the files to PCBWay, and they can be used for production after being reviewed by the staff. Note: If you want to place an assembly order, please be sure to add MPN information to the BOM. This can help the quoter source the devices you need more accurately. Manual installation Except for the way mentioned before, you can also download the latest ZIP file from https://github.com/pcbway/PCBWay-Fabrication-Toolkit-for-KiCad: Open the "Plugin and Content Manager" from the main window of KiCad and install the ZIP file via "Install from File". About BOM Through BOM files, we can get all information of the components used in your design. In order to speed up the quotation process, we need this information: 1. Designator (necessary) 2. Quantity (necessary) 3. MPN/Part Number (necessary) 4. Package/Footprint (necessary) 5. Manufacturer (optional) 6. Description/value (optional) If you have more suggestions, please leave a message below, PCBWay has committed to providing everyone with high-quality services. Verify Now Blog > PCBWay Plug-In for OpenSCAD PCBWay Plug-In for OpenSCAD by: PCBWay Oct 24,2024 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in News We are excited to announce that we have welcomed a new partner! PCBWay has recently collaborated with OpenSCAD to integrate the PCBWay plug-in into the software. This means that from now on, users can directly jump to the PCBWay page from OpenSCAD to place orders, which will greatly improve the efficiency of pre-production preparation work. OpenSCAD download link ( https://openscad.org/ ) After completing the design in OpenSCAD, click Design -> 3D print. In the newly popped-up dialog box, select PCBWay, and then click OK. Then it will be automatically redirected to PCBWay's 3D printing pricing page. After selecting the parameters, you can submit your order. That's how the PCBWay plug-in in OpenSCAD is used. Verify Now Blog > PCB Design Layout Guidelines for Routing PCB Design Layout Guidelines for Routing by: Mia Jul 17,2024 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout PCB Design Guideline PCB Routing PCB Layout 1. Length Control in Routing Length controlling is very important in PCB design. The traces should be kept as short as possible to avoid introducing unnecessary interference due to excessive length. For important signal traces, such as clock signal traces, be sure to place its oscillator very close to the device. 2. Direction Control in Routing The routing directions of adjacent layers should be orthogonal to avoid the signal traces of adjacent layers running in the same direction, thus reducing unnecessary crosstalk between layers. 3. Rules for Chamfer Sharp angles and right angles should be avoided in PCB design, otherwise, unnecessary radiation will be generated and the process performance will be poor. 4. Open Loop Detection in Routing Generally, dangling lines are not allowed. This is mainly to avoid the "antenna effect" and reduce unnecessary interference radiation and reception. Otherwise, serious consequences may occur. 5. Try to Avoid Self-loop Routing When designing PCB, we should pay attention to the situation where signal traces form self-loops between different layers. Especially when routing multi-layer boards, signal traces are routed between layers, which has a greater chance of forming self-loops. Self-loops can cause radiation interference. 6. Rules for Ground Loop The minimal loop rule states that the loop area formed by a signal trace and its return path should be as small as possible. The smaller the loop area, the less external radiation it emits and the less interference it receives from the outside. 7. Rules for the Integrity of Power and Ground Layers For areas with dense vias, care should be taken to avoid the holes connecting to each other in the hollowed-out areas of the power and ground layers, which would segment the plane layer. This may destroy the integrity of the plane layer and further increase the loop area of ​​the signal trace in the ground layer. 8. 3W Rule In order to reduce crosstalk between traces, the trace spacing should be large enough. When the center-to-center distance between traces is at least three times the space width, 70% of the electric field will not interfere with each other, known as the 3W rule. To achieve 98% of the electric field not interfering with each other, a 10W spacing can be used. 9. Shielding Protection Shielding protection corresponds to the ground loop rule, which is actually to minimize the loop area of ​​the signal. It is more common in some important signals, such as clock signals and synchronization signals. For some particularly important, high-frequency signals, a coaxial cable shielding design should be considered. This involves isolating the signal traces with ground traces on all sides (top, bottom, left, and right). Additionally, careful consideration must be given to how effectively to connect the shield ground to the actual ground plane. 10. Rules for Impedance Matching Check The routing width in the same network should be kept consistent. Changes in trace width can cause non-uniform characteristic impedance of the circuit, leading to reflections when the transmission speed is high. This should be avoided in the design whenever possible. Under certain conditions, such as structures similar to lead-out traces of connectors or the lead-out traces of BGA packages, changes in trace width may be unavoidable, so the effective length of the inconsistent sections should be minimized. 11. Rules for Overlapping Power and Ground Layers Different power layers should avoid overlapping in space to reduce interference between different power supplies. This is especially important for power supplies with significantly different voltages. If it is difficult to avoid, consider placing a ground plane in between. 12. 20H Principle To prevent board edge radiation, the power plane should be retracted during design. Using H (the dielectric thickness between the power and ground) as a unit, a retraction of 20H can confine 70% of the electric field within the edge of the ground layer, while a retraction of 100H can confine 98% of the electric field within it. Verify Now Blog > HDI PCB Layout Guide for High Speed Optical Module PCB Design HDI PCB Layout Guide for High Speed Optical Module PCB Design by: Mila Sep 03,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout hdi pcb HDI pcb design optical module pcb high speed pcb layout An optical module PCB is a typical high-frequency, high-density HDI PCB precision board. Its material selection is closely related to transmission rate, link length, loss budget, and device platforms. While 10G and lower modules can use materials like high-Tg FR-4, high-speed modules operating at 25G, 56G, 100G, 400G, and 800G impose stringent requirements on low-loss materials, impedance control, and manufacturing consistency. Below are seven core layout design points and key differences compared to standard PCBs, focusing on high speed pcb layout and practical signal integrity engineering without rigid design fallacies. 1. Substrate Selection and StackUp Design Substrate selection and layer stackup form the foundation for stable high-frequency transmission, directly determining link insertion loss, impedance accuracy, and signal integrity. Multi-Dimensional Rate-Matched Selection: For 25G+ channels, select substrates considering Nyquist frequency, link length, insertion loss budget, dielectric loss, copper foil roughness, and stackup. For long-distance or low-loss channels, choose mid-to-low loss high-speed substrates. Non-critical areas like low-speed control and power can use high-Tg FR-4 to balance performance and cost on an optical module PCB. Adjacent Reference Ground Planes: High-speed differential signal layers should adopt a "signal-reference ground" structure to minimize edge-field coupling. Power layers should pair with adjacent ground layers to optimize PDN impedance via inter-layer capacitance. Pre-Simulation Impedance Modeling: Determine stackup parameters early through SI simulation. The industry standard target is typically 100 ohms differential impedance, with high-performance channels strictly controlling tolerances within +/- 5%. 2. High-Speed Differential TX/RX Signal Integrity High-speed differential signals are the core of data transmission in an optical module PCB. Design should focus on eliminating geometric discontinuities and parasitic interference. Symmetry and Equal Length: Match trace widths, spacing, bends, and via layouts for differential pairs. Advanced HDI pcb design requires controlling intra-pair length skew to prevent differential-to-common mode noise conversion. Trace Geometry Continuity: Use 45-degree angles or smooth arc transitions instead of rigid 90-degree turns. High-frequency reflections stem mostly from vias, pads, stubs, and split reference planes rather than standard trace corners. Minimal Via Structures and Stub Optimization: Minimize layer transitions. For long through-hole structures, apply back-drilling to remove residual stubs, cutting down reflections and resonances. （Backdrill + Via Stub） Unbroken High-Frequency Return Paths: Avoid routing differential traces across ground splits or slot gaps. Provide nearby stitching ground vias whenever signals switch layers. (Differential Pair + Reference Plane + Return Path) Crosstalk Mitigation: Apply the 3W rule during initial layout for proper spacing. For 112G PAM4 ultra-high-speed scenarios, refine trace spacing with 3D EM simulation and add ground via shielding walls where necessary. 3. Optoelectronic Isolation and Sensitive Layout Optical modules combine sensitive analog signals with high-speed digital logic. The analog front-end requires isolation from power and digital noise. Physical Isolation: Separate TOSA/ROSA components and TIA analog circuits from high-speed digital traces and switching power supplies based on form factors (SFP, QSFP, OSFP). Short Analog Traces: Keep weak analog traces from optical devices to TIA and driver ICs as short as possible, avoiding parallel routing alongside high-speed digital lines. Analog Circuit Shielding: Implement localized ground shielding or small metal shields around laser drivers and TIA circuits to isolate high-frequency digital noise. 4. Power Integrity (PI) Optimization Focus on low-impedance return paths, minimal current loops, and sub-region noise reduction. Minimal Loop Decoupling: Configure decoupling networks based on target PDN impedance. Place capacitors close to power pins to minimize parasitic inductance. Solid Ground Plane Priority: Maintain a continuous, low-impedance ground plane across the HDI PCB to provide a solid reference. Apply localized filtering for sensitive analog zones rather than single-point star grounding across the board. Thermal Copper Pour for Power Chips: Place large copper areas with thermal via arrays beneath heat-generating components like laser drivers to disperse heat quickly. 5. Thermal Management in HDI PCB Design Optical module DSPs, optical drivers, and laser diodes generate concentrated heat. High temperatures cause device aging, DK/Df parameter drift, and impedance shifts. Efficient Thermal Paths: Place dense thermal via arrays under high-power devices (DSP, TOSA) to transfer heat from the optical module PCB inner layers to the metal housing. Hot/Cold Component Partitioning: Isolate heat sources from temperature-sensitive optical and clock components to prevent thermal drift and premature aging. Symmetrical Design against Warpage: Balance copper distribution and layer stack-ups across the HDI PCB to manage thermal-mechanical stress during reflow soldering. （Thermal Path IC → Thermal Via → Copper Plane → Housing） 6. EMC and Grounding for High Speed PCB Layout Symmetrical Routing for Common-Mode Noise: Maintain structural symmetry in high-speed differential traces to reduce EMI radiation. Connect the module metal shell to the PCB ground for low-impedance shielding. Interface ESD Protection : Place TVS diodes and common-mode chokes near edge connectors to route ESD currents quickly to chassis ground. Isolate Interference Sources: Keep power inductors and switching regulators away from sensitive RX analog inputs to prevent magnetic coupling. 7. DFM Guidelines for Optical Module PCB Manufacturing Precise HDI pcb design and assembly standards ensure manufacturing yield for dense components. Precision Soldering Design: Use Via-in-Pad or micro-vias for high-density BGAs. For QFN thermal pads, use segmented stencil openings to reduce solder voiding and floating. Optical Alignment Tolerance: Match mechanical outline and mounting hole tolerances precisely with metal housings to avoid optical misalignments. Test Points and Gold Fingers: Keep test points off high-speed trunk lines. Use hard gold plating for edge connector gold fingers to ensure durability across insertion cycles. 8.Optical Module PCB vs Standard PCB Core Differences Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > How to Properly Handle Unused IC Pins in Schematic Design How to Properly Handle Unused IC Pins in Schematic Design by: Mila Sep 09,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout schematic design cmos pins nc pins When working on schematic design , engineers often encounter situations like this: to meet the core functional requirements, a 100-pin MCU is selected, but only 60 pins are actually used. Or a 4-channel op-amp is selected, but only three channels are needed. Some ICs may also have pins marked as NC. Seeing all those pins labeled as "Not Connected" on the schematic can be confusing. Should these unused pins simply be left floating? Should they be connected to ground? Or should they be connected to a power supply? Improper handling of unused pins can lead to undefined input states, increased power consumption, or noise interference, and in severe cases may even affect device reliability. This article explains how to properly handle these seemingly minor but important details in schematic design. 1. Why Should Unused IC Pins Be Handled Carefully? Many ICs today use CMOS technology. One key rule to remember is: do not leave CMOS inputs floating, especially digital input pins. （CMOS device） This can be understood from the internal structure of CMOS circuits. A typical CMOS input stage consists of an inverter made up of a PMOS and an NMOS connected in series. When the input is low, the PMOS is on and the NMOS is off. When the input is high, the PMOS is off and the NMOS is on. Under ideal static conditions, only a very small leakage current flows, giving CMOS circuits very low static power consumption. 2. What Happens When CMOS Pins Are Left Floating? What happens when an input is left floating? Because the input has very high impedance, it can easily be affected by surrounding electromagnetic noise, parasitic coupling, and leakage current. As a result, the input voltage may become undefined and fluctuate between low and high levels. When the input voltage falls within the transition region of the CMOS input stage, the PMOS and NMOS may both be partially turned on, causing increased supply current. In other words, floating CMOS pins have no guaranteed logic state, so it is impossible to reliably determine whether the input will be interpreted as a high or low level. 3. How to Handle Unused MCU GPIOs? Modern MCUs usually provide multifunctional GPIOs. For unused GPIOs, follow the requirements in the device datasheet and configure the corresponding IO as an output with a defined state, such as driving it low or high. If supported by the device, it can also be configured as an input with an internal pull-up or pull-down. When permitted by the device, this eliminates the need for external pull-up or pull-down resistors, saving components and PCB space. For critical pins such as interrupt, reset, and mode-selection pins, however, their default logic states should be clearly defined. Whether an external pull-up or pull-down resistor is required should be determined according to the datasheet and reference design to prevent unintended triggering. 4. How to Handle Unused Op-Amp Channels? Op-amps and ADCs require special attention because analog circuits are more sensitive to noise, and their unused pins may need to be handled differently from digital circuits. For example, if you use a dual-channel op-amp but only need one channel, what should you do with the unused channel? （IC Pins） Leaving it floating is generally not recommended because the input pins can pick up noise, causing the output to saturate and potentially increasing power consumption. What if both the non-inverting and inverting inputs are connected to ground? This puts the op-amp in an open-loop configuration, so its output may not be well controlled. For a typical voltage-feedback op-amp, if permitted by the datasheet, a better approach is to configure the unused channel as a voltage follower: connect the output to the inverting input to create negative feedback, and connect the non-inverting input to GND. However, the op-amp's input common-mode range and output swing must also be checked to ensure that this configuration is within the device's specifications. 5. What About Unused ADC Inputs? Unused ADC channels should be handled according to the device datasheet. Some devices recommend connecting unused ADC inputs to GND or another stable reference level to prevent the channel from picking up noise. However, directly connecting the input to ground should not be treated as a universal rule for all ADCs. Therefore, unused ADC inputs should not simply be treated in the same way as digital GPIOs. Always check the manufacturer's recommended connection method before finalizing the schematic design. 6. What Do NC Pins Mean on an IC? IC datasheets often contain pins marked as NC, or "No Connect." These NC pins need to be examined carefully. NC does not necessarily mean that the pin can be connected in any way. Some NC pins may have no internal connection and should simply be left floating. However, other pins marked as NC may have internal connections related to testing, reserved functions, or other circuits. The handling method must strictly follow the datasheet. For example, some datasheets specify "Must be left floating," while others specify "Must be tied to GND." If you connect NC pins to ground without checking the datasheet, you could potentially cause unexpected behavior or interfere with internal test or reserved functions. 7. The Key Rule: Always Check the Datasheet When dealing with unused IC pins, the most important principle is not simply whether a pin should be left floating or connected to ground. Instead, first identify the pin type and then follow the connection requirements specified in the datasheet. （DBV package） Different types of GPIOs, analog inputs, op-amp channels, and NC pins may require completely different handling methods. In simple terms: Unused GPIOs: Configure them to a defined state according to the datasheet. Critical input pins: Make sure they have a clearly defined default logic level. Unused op-amp channels: Use a stable negative-feedback configuration when recommended. Unused ADC inputs: Follow the device manufacturer's recommended connection method. NC pins: Strictly follow the datasheet requirements. A simple "Not Connected" label on a schematic may involve power consumption, noise, stability, and even device reliability. Do not rely on assumptions. Check the datasheet first, then decide how the pin should be connected. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > How to Properly Handle Unused IC Pins in Schematic Design How to Properly Handle Unused IC Pins in Schematic Design by: Mila Sep 09,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout schematic design cmos pins nc pins When working on schematic design , engineers often encounter situations like this: to meet the core functional requirements, a 100-pin MCU is selected, but only 60 pins are actually used. Or a 4-channel op-amp is selected, but only three channels are needed. Some ICs may also have pins marked as NC. Seeing all those pins labeled as "Not Connected" on the schematic can be confusing. Should these unused pins simply be left floating? Should they be connected to ground? Or should they be connected to a power supply? Improper handling of unused pins can lead to undefined input states, increased power consumption, or noise interference, and in severe cases may even affect device reliability. This article explains how to properly handle these seemingly minor but important details in schematic design. 1. Why Should Unused IC Pins Be Handled Carefully? Many ICs today use CMOS technology. One key rule to remember is: do not leave CMOS inputs floating, especially digital input pins. （CMOS device） This can be understood from the internal structure of CMOS circuits. A typical CMOS input stage consists of an inverter made up of a PMOS and an NMOS connected in series. When the input is low, the PMOS is on and the NMOS is off. When the input is high, the PMOS is off and the NMOS is on. Under ideal static conditions, only a very small leakage current flows, giving CMOS circuits very low static power consumption. 2. What Happens When CMOS Pins Are Left Floating? What happens when an input is left floating? Because the input has very high impedance, it can easily be affected by surrounding electromagnetic noise, parasitic coupling, and leakage current. As a result, the input voltage may become undefined and fluctuate between low and high levels. When the input voltage falls within the transition region of the CMOS input stage, the PMOS and NMOS may both be partially turned on, causing increased supply current. In other words, floating CMOS pins have no guaranteed logic state, so it is impossible to reliably determine whether the input will be interpreted as a high or low level. 3. How to Handle Unused MCU GPIOs? Modern MCUs usually provide multifunctional GPIOs. For unused GPIOs, follow the requirements in the device datasheet and configure the corresponding IO as an output with a defined state, such as driving it low or high. If supported by the device, it can also be configured as an input with an internal pull-up or pull-down. When permitted by the device, this eliminates the need for external pull-up or pull-down resistors, saving components and PCB space. For critical pins such as interrupt, reset, and mode-selection pins, however, their default logic states should be clearly defined. Whether an external pull-up or pull-down resistor is required should be determined according to the datasheet and reference design to prevent unintended triggering. 4. How to Handle Unused Op-Amp Channels? Op-amps and ADCs require special attention because analog circuits are more sensitive to noise, and their unused pins may need to be handled differently from digital circuits. For example, if you use a dual-channel op-amp but only need one channel, what should you do with the unused channel? （IC Pins） Leaving it floating is generally not recommended because the input pins can pick up noise, causing the output to saturate and potentially increasing power consumption. What if both the non-inverting and inverting inputs are connected to ground? This puts the op-amp in an open-loop configuration, so its output may not be well controlled. For a typical voltage-feedback op-amp, if permitted by the datasheet, a better approach is to configure the unused channel as a voltage follower: connect the output to the inverting input to create negative feedback, and connect the non-inverting input to GND. However, the op-amp's input common-mode range and output swing must also be checked to ensure that this configuration is within the device's specifications. 5. What About Unused ADC Inputs? Unused ADC channels should be handled according to the device datasheet. Some devices recommend connecting unused ADC inputs to GND or another stable reference level to prevent the channel from picking up noise. However, directly connecting the input to ground should not be treated as a universal rule for all ADCs. Therefore, unused ADC inputs should not simply be treated in the same way as digital GPIOs. Always check the manufacturer's recommended connection method before finalizing the schematic design. 6. What Do NC Pins Mean on an IC? IC datasheets often contain pins marked as NC, or "No Connect." These NC pins need to be examined carefully. NC does not necessarily mean that the pin can be connected in any way. Some NC pins may have no internal connection and should simply be left floating. However, other pins marked as NC may have internal connections related to testing, reserved functions, or other circuits. The handling method must strictly follow the datasheet. For example, some datasheets specify "Must be left floating," while others specify "Must be tied to GND." If you connect NC pins to ground without checking the datasheet, you could potentially cause unexpected behavior or interfere with internal test or reserved functions. 7. The Key Rule: Always Check the Datasheet When dealing with unused IC pins, the most important principle is not simply whether a pin should be left floating or connected to ground. Instead, first identify the pin type and then follow the connection requirements specified in the datasheet. （DBV package） Different types of GPIOs, analog inputs, op-amp channels, and NC pins may require completely different handling methods. In simple terms: Unused GPIOs: Configure them to a defined state according to the datasheet. Critical input pins: Make sure they have a clearly defined default logic level. Unused op-amp channels: Use a stable negative-feedback configuration when recommended. Unused ADC inputs: Follow the device manufacturer's recommended connection method. NC pins: Strictly follow the datasheet requirements. A simple "Not Connected" label on a schematic may involve power consumption, noise, stability, and even device reliability. Do not rely on assumptions. Check the datasheet first, then decide how the pin should be connected. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > USB Type-C Design and CC Pin Configuration: A Practical Hardware Design Guide USB Type-C Design and CC Pin Configuration: A Practical Hardware Design Guide by: Mila Sep 08,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout hardware design type c design usb design usb type c design usb pcb design One of the most common pitfalls in Hardware Design for Type-C interfaces is confusing the legacy protocols used by USB-A ports with the native USB Type-C protocol. Some designers mistakenly treat D+ / D− as the core charging detection pins of Type-C, which can lead to design failures. The voltage is a normal 5V, the polarity is correct, but the device still does not charge, fails to be recognized, only works in one plug orientation, or has limited charging current. Compatibility issues may also occur with some phones. In many cases, there is basically one reason: CC1 and CC2 are not connected correctly. Let's look at the most common 5V Type-C charging configuration. Once you understand it, you can use it directly in your Type C Design. 1. The Most Important Conclusion For a Type-C interface, CC1 / CC2 are the core channels for power role detection, connection detection, current capability detection, and USB PD communication. D+ and D− do not handle basic Type-C power detection or USB PD negotiation in a standard C-to-C connection. This is one of the key differences between traditional USB and modern USB Type C Design: CC pins: The dedicated Type-C configuration channel used for power role detection, connection detection, plug orientation detection, Type-C current capability detection, and USB PD communication. D+ / D− pins: Mainly used for USB 2.0 data transmission and compatibility with certain legacy charging protocols, such as BC1.2. In simple terms: C-to-C charging: Basic power detection mainly relies on CC, not D+ / D−. A-to-C charging: Legacy USB-A charging protocols may use D+ / D− for charging detection. 2. Why Does C-to-C Charging Mainly Rely on CC? Taking a standard USB-C-to-USB-C charging connection as an example, the Source and Sink first establish a connection through the CC pins. The basic process is: 1. The charger provides Rp pull-ups on CC1 and CC2. 2. The phone or other powered device uses Rd pull-downs to indicate that it is a Sink. 3. The two sides detect the connection and determine the available Type-C current capability through CC. 4. If both sides support USB PD, they can further communicate through the CC channel to negotiate voltage, current, and power. It is important to note that 56KΩ, 22KΩ, and 10KΩ Rp values correspond to different advertised current capabilities. They should not be interpreted as “56KΩ directly unlocks 5V/3A.” Therefore, Type-C current capability detection and USB PD fast charging should be distinguished: Type-C current capability detection → Rp / Rd USB PD power negotiation → PD communication over CC D+ / D− mainly handle USB 2.0 data and certain legacy charging protocols. 3. CC vs. D+ / D−: What Does Each One Actually Do? CC1 / CC2: The Core Type-C Power and Connection Pins CC stands for Configuration Channel and is an important feature that distinguishes USB Type-C from traditional USB-A interfaces. CC1 and CC2 are mainly responsible for: Power role detection: Rp indicates a Source, while Rd indicates a Sink. Connection detection: Determines whether a valid connection has been established. Plug orientation detection: The active CC pin helps determine the plug orientation. Type-C current capability detection: The Source uses Rp to advertise its power capability. USB PD communication: USB PD devices use the CC channel to negotiate voltage, current, and power. Therefore, in a standard Type-C C-to-C power connection: Correct CC configuration is critical to proper device detection and power delivery. This is why CC routing and component placement are important in USB PCB Design. D+ / D−: Data Transmission and Legacy Charging Compatibility D+ / D− are essentially USB 2.0 differential data lines. They are mainly used for: 1. USB 2.0 data transmission, programming, and communication 2. Compatibility with certain legacy USB-A charging protocols For example, USB BC1.2 charging detection mechanisms may use D+ / D−. The key distinction is: C-to-C architecture: Basic Type-C power detection relies on CC. A-to-C architecture: Legacy USB-A charging protocols may involve D+ / D−. Therefore, the fact that D+ / D− were widely used for charging detection in the USB-A era does not mean that they are required for basic charging in a USB-C-to-USB-C connection. This distinction is important in practical USB Design . 4. Three Common CC Configurations + Applicable Scenarios The most common Type-C CC configurations can be divided into three categories: Sink, Source, and DRP. Typical resistor values include: Rp = 56KΩ / 22KΩ / 10KΩ Rd = 5.1KΩ The exact configuration depends on the device role and the Type-C / USB PD requirements. Configuration 1: Dual 5.1KΩ Pull-Down Resistors on CC1 / CC2 Typical connection: CC1 → 5.1KΩ → GND CC2 → 5.1KΩ → GND Applicable to: Phones, development boards, microcontroller boards, small appliances, and other Type-C devices that work as Sink devices. Function: The device indicates that it is a powered device, allowing the Source to detect the connection and determine the plug orientation. For basic Type-C power, this configuration can support standard 5V operation. Note: Two 5.1KΩ resistors do not automatically give the device USB PD fast-charging capability. If the device needs 9V, 12V, 15V, 20V, or other USB PD voltages, an appropriate USB PD Controller and supporting power-management circuitry are normally required. （Pull-Down Resistors） Configuration 2: Dual Rp Pull-Up Resistors on CC1 / CC2 Typical connection: CC1 → Rp → VBUS CC2 → Rp → VBUS Applicable to: Standard USB Type-C chargers, power banks with Type-C output ports, and other devices that work as a Source. Function: The Source uses CC to advertise its power capability so that the connected Type-C device can identify the power source. Different Rp configurations correspond to different Type-C default current capabilities. If USB PD fast charging is required, the design needs to support PD communication through the CC channel rather than relying on Rp alone. If compatibility with legacy USB-A charging protocols is also required, additional D+ / D− charging-detection circuitry or a charging protocol IC can be added according to the product requirements. （Pull-Up Resistors） Configuration 3: Dynamic Rp / Rd Switching for DRP Applicable to: Expansion docks, power banks, portable energy-storage devices, and other Type-C devices that need to dynamically switch between Source and Sink roles. Function: The device can determine its role according to the connected device and connection state, allowing it to operate as either a power source or a powered device. Note: DRP does not simply mean connecting Rp and Rd to CC1 / CC2 at the same time. In practical designs, a Type-C Controller or USB PD Controller is typically used to dynamically manage Rp / Rd, together with power-path control for safe bidirectional power delivery. （Rp / Rd Switching Resistors） Configuration 4: Type-C + USB PD Controller for Fast Charging If the product needs more than basic 5V power, such as: 9V / 12V / 15V / 20V or needs: Voltage, current, and power negotiation then Rp / Rd resistors alone are not sufficient. A typical architecture is: CC1 / CC2 → USB PD Controller → Power Path / DC-DC The PD Controller communicates through the CC channel and controls the downstream power circuitry according to the negotiated power profile. For USB Type C Design , this distinction is important when moving from basic 5V charging to USB PD fast charging. 5. A Common Mistake: Do Not Simply Short CC1 and CC2 Together Some Type-C designs try to make the interface work in both orientations by simply connecting: CC1 + CC2 → Shorted → One Rp or Rd. This should not be treated as a standard Type-C CC configuration. Simply shorting CC1 and CC2 can cause problems with proper connection detection and orientation handling, and may lead to compatibility issues in some applications. This is especially important for designs involving USB PD, higher current levels, or E-Marker cables. The correct approach is to configure the CC pins according to the required device role: Sink: CC1 → Rd CC2 → Rd Source: CC1 → Rp CC2 → Rp DRP: CC1 / CC2 → Type-C / PD Controller for dynamic role management Therefore, in USB PCB Design, CC1 and CC2 should be treated as separate configuration paths rather than simply tying them together. （CC1 and CC2 are shorted） 6. Final Takeaway: Check CC Before D+ / D− If you are designing a basic Type-C 5V Sink interface, the first thing to remember is simple: CC1 and CC2 each use a 5.1KΩ pull-down resistor to GND. For a Type-C Source, select the appropriate Rp configuration according to the required power capability. If the product requires: Bidirectional charging → DRP 9V / 12V / 15V / 20V → USB PD Higher-current applications → Consider USB PD, cable capability, E-Marker requirements, and the complete power path D+ / D− should be determined separately according to whether the product needs: USB 2.0 data transmissionOr Legacy USB-A charging protocol compatibility. The biggest pitfall in Type-C Hardware Design is not simply whether VBUS measures 5V. The key is whether the interface correctly follows the USB Type-C rules for CC1 / CC2, Rp, Rd, DRP, and USB PD. Once these concepts are clear, basic Type-C charging interfaces become much easier to design correctly. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. If compatibility with legacy USB-A charging protocols is also required, additional D+ / D− charging-detection circuitry or a charging protocol IC can be added according to the product requirements. （Pull-Up Resistors） Configuration 3: Dynamic Rp / Rd Switching for DRP Applicable to: Expansion docks, power banks, portable energy-storage devices, and other Type-C devices that need to dynamically switch between Source and Sink roles. Function: The device can determine its role according to the connected device and connection state, allowing it to operate as either a power source or a powered device. Note: DRP does not simply mean connecting Rp and Rd to CC1 / CC2 at the same time. In practical designs, a Type-C Controller or USB PD Controller is typically used to dynamically manage Rp / Rd, together with power-path control for safe bidirectional power delivery. （Rp / Rd Switching Resistors） Configuration 4: Type-C + USB PD Controller for Fast Charging If the product needs more than basic 5V power, such as: 9V / 12V / 15V / 20V or needs: Voltage, current, and power negotiation then Rp / Rd resistors alone are not sufficient. A typical architecture is: CC1 / CC2 → USB PD Controller → Power Path / DC-DC The PD Controller communicates through the CC channel and controls the downstream power circuitry according to the negotiated power profile. For USB Type C Design , this distinction is important when moving from basic 5V charging to USB PD fast charging. 5. A Common Mistake: Do Not Simply Short CC1 and CC2 Together Some Type-C designs try to make the interface work in both orientations by simply connecting: CC1 + CC2 → Shorted → One Rp or Rd. This should not be treated as a standard Type-C CC configuration. Simply shorting CC1 and CC2 can cause problems with proper connection detection and orientation handling, and may lead to compatibility issues in some applications. This is especially important for designs involving USB PD, higher current levels, or E-Marker cables. The correct approach is to configure the CC pins according to the required device role: Sink: CC1 → Rd CC2 → Rd Source: CC1 → Rp CC2 → Rp DRP: CC1 / CC2 → Type-C / PD Controller for dynamic role management Therefore, in USB PCB Design, CC1 and CC2 should be treated as separate configuration paths rather than simply tying them together. （CC1 and CC2 are shorted） 6. Final Takeaway: Check CC Before D+ / D− If you are designing a basic Type-C 5V Sink interface, the first thing to remember is simple: CC1 and CC2 each use a 5.1KΩ pull-down resistor to GND. For a Type-C Source, select the appropriate Rp configuration according to the required power capability. If the product requires: Bidirectional charging → DRP 9V / 12V / 15V / 20V → USB PD Higher-current applications → Consider USB PD, cable capability, E-Marker requirements, and the complete power path D+ / D− should be determined separately according to whether the product needs: USB 2.0 data transmissionOr Legacy USB-A charging protocol compatibility. The biggest pitfall in Type-C Hardware Design is not simply whether VBUS measures 5V. The key is whether the interface correctly follows the USB Type-C rules for CC1 / CC2, Rp, Rd, DRP, and USB PD. Once these concepts are clear, basic Type-C charging interfaces become much easier to design correctly. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > PCB Impedance Control Guide: How to Fix Impedance Discontinuities in PCB Layout PCB Impedance Control Guide: How to Fix Impedance Discontinuities in PCB Layout by: Mila Aug 31,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout impedance control pcb design pcb layout pcb impedance control In modern pcb design, maintaining signal integrity relies on a stable transmission path. Proper impedance control prevents signal reflection and ensures stable performance across your board. This article explores why pcb impedance control is essential, where discontinuities typically occur during pcb layout, and how targeted optimizations improve overall channel quality. 1. Why Impedance Control Matters Why do we need pcb impedance control, how do we achieve it, and which aspects require adjustments? The simulation results below tell the story—showing schematics with and without impedance matching. When impedance mismatch occurs across a transmission link, signals reflect at points of impedance discontinuity. These reflected signals combine with original signals, resulting in waveform anomalies like overshoot, undershoot, ringing, and glitches. Heavy reflection can cause false sampling at the receiver, compromising high-speed system stability. Effective impedance control requires precise stackup planning. Before routing your high-speed signals, make sure to test your trace impedance with our free online calculator to determine the exact trace width and spacing needed. 2. Key Areas for Impedance Optimization From the IC package interior to PCB traces and receiver ICs, high-speed links contain multiple regions vulnerable to impedance mismatch. Common risk areas include: IC package pads BGA breakout routing Layer-change vias Termination resistors, capacitors, and connector pads Differential pair length matching Discontinuous return paths Discontinuous reference planes Stubs and branch trace routing Impedance discontinuities often occur near IC package pads. While design space here is limited, keeping thin traces short and adding ground cutouts (anti-pads) under adjacent layers can slightly raise impedance—a approach often seen in PCIe Gen5 design guidelines. Impedance shifts also happen after signal lines exit the IC through capacitors, resistors, vias, and connectors. TDR data clearly demonstrates the difference before and after optimization. During length matching, inevitable small serpentines on differential pairs can trigger local impedance disruptions. Length compensation segments should be placed in areas with controlled impedance environments, continuous reference planes, and safe distances from sensitive structures like vias or pads. For regions with structural discontinuities, combine topology planning with SI simulation for co-optimization rather than blindly adding serpentine traces along continuous mainlines. Disrupted return paths cause impedance drops and ground bounce. When high-speed signals change layers without nearby ground stitching vias, returning current is forced to detour. This increases loop area, parasitic inductance, electromagnetic field shifts, crosstalk, EMI risks, and impedance mismatch. The diagram below shows an impedance jump caused by a reference plane discontinuity. When traces cross reference plane splits, slots, or other discontinuous regions, the original return path is disrupted. This alters the local transmission line structure, creating impedance mismatch and additional signal integrity risks during pcb layout . The diagram below shows an impedance jump caused by a stub. 3. Benefits of Impedance Optimization The points mentioned above are mostly locations where impedance discontinuities occur along the link. Below is a data comparison of an entire high-speed differential transmission line before and after optimization. The link includes various impedance discontinuity points, such as IC pin output pads, layer-change vias, capacitors, load-end connectors, and stubs. By optimizing discontinuous impedance structures within the link—including pads, vias, passive components, connectors, and stubs—local signal reflections are reduced, and the channel's return loss performance is significantly improved. In this case, after the impedance structures were optimized, the channel's insertion loss also improved, demonstrating that mitigating severe structural discontinuities helps enhance the overall performance of high-speed channels in pcb design. 4. Practical Optimization Methods Proper pcb design requires systematic approaches across different elements. The following sections outline practical optimization workflows for passive components (based on 4-layer 1.6mm stackups), vias, and length-matching techniques essential for modern pcb layout: (Note: The following optimization case uses a 4-layer, 1.6 mm total thickness PCB as an example. Actual impedance cannot be determined solely by total board thickness; it must be calculated and verified using dielectric thickness, copper thickness, material Dk, trace width/spacing, and target impedance.) Verify Now Blog > PCB Layout Design Process from Schematic to Manufacturing PCB Layout Design Process from Schematic to Manufacturing by: Mila Sep 16,2025 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout pcb layout design schematic design pcb layout services pcb layout design services PCB layout design is the process of transforming an electrical schematic into a complete, manufacturable printed circuit board (PCB). A well-designed PCB layout must do more than simply connect components. It needs to balance electrical performance, signal integrity, power integrity, thermal management, mechanical constraints, manufacturability, and reliability. For complex electronic products, decisions made during PCB layout can have a significant impact on product performance, production yield, cost, and time to market. A professional PCB layout workflow therefore requires systematic planning, engineering review, design verification, and manufacturing preparation. Below is an overview of the PCB layout design process we follow, from the initial schematic review to final manufacturing data.You can also find more information on our PCB Layout page . Step 1 – Design Preparation and Engineering Review The PCB layout process begins with a detailed review of the design requirements and source files. Before starting the layout, our engineers review the schematic and project specifications to make sure the design is ready for PCB implementation. This includes checking: Schematic completeness and connectivity Component information and footprints Board dimensions and mechanical constraints Layer count and stack-up requirements Component placement restrictions High-speed and differential signals Power distribution requirements Impedance-control requirements Thermal considerations Manufacturing capabilities and design rules If the customer only provides a PDF or image-based schematic, we can recreate the schematic in professional EDA software before proceeding with PCB layout. If the original schematic file is available, we can directly import the design data, generate the netlist, and establish the PCB design environment. At this stage, we also identify potential design issues that could affect layout, manufacturing, or product performance. Resolving these issues early helps reduce design iterations later in the process. Step 2 – PCB Stack-Up and Design Rule Setup Before component placement and routing, the PCB layer structure and key design rules need to be established. For multilayer and high-speed PCBs, the stack-up directly affects signal integrity, impedance control, power integrity, EMI performance, and manufacturability. Depending on the application, we may define: Number of PCB layers Core and prepreg materials Copper thickness Dielectric thickness Controlled impedance requirements Power and ground reference planes Minimum trace width and spacing Via structures and drill sizes Manufacturing constraints For high-speed designs, impedance-controlled traces and their reference planes are considered from the beginning rather than being treated as an afterthought. The design rules are then configured in the EDA software to ensure that the layout remains consistent with both the electrical requirements and the PCB manufacturer's manufacturing capabilities. Step 3 – Component Placement Component placement is one of the most important stages of PCB layout because it establishes the physical structure of the entire board. The placement strategy typically starts with components whose locations are constrained by the mechanical design, such as: Connectors Switches and buttons Mounting holes Displays Mechanical interfaces Heat sinks and other thermal components Core components such as MCUs, CPUs, FPGAs, memory devices, power ICs, and communication ICs are then positioned according to signal flow, functional relationships, and electrical requirements. Supporting components are placed close to their corresponding devices to minimize unnecessary routing length and improve electrical performance. During placement, we consider several factors simultaneously: Signal Integrity High-speed interfaces and sensitive signals require appropriate component relationships and short, well-controlled routing paths. Power Integrity Decoupling capacitors should be positioned close to the relevant power pins, while power distribution paths should be kept short and low impedance. Thermal Management Heat-generating components need sufficient copper area, thermal vias, airflow consideration, and appropriate spacing from temperature-sensitive devices. EMI/EMC Performance Sensitive analog circuits, high-speed digital circuits, switching power supplies, and other potential noise sources need to be appropriately positioned to reduce interference. Manufacturability Component spacing, assembly orientation, soldering requirements, and accessibility for inspection and rework are also considered. A well-planned placement makes subsequent routing more efficient while improving the overall reliability and manufacturability of the PCB. Step 4 – PCB Routing Once the component placement is finalized, the next stage is PCB routing. Routing is not simply about finding a path between two pads. The routing strategy must consider electrical performance, signal integrity, power distribution, EMI/EMC, and manufacturing constraints. Depending on the design, routing priorities may include: High-Speed and Critical Signals High-speed interfaces such as USB, DDR, PCIe, Ethernet, HDMI, LVDS, and other differential interfaces may require: Controlled impedance Differential-pair routing Length matching Skew control Appropriate reference planes Minimized discontinuities Careful via transitions Critical signals are routed according to their electrical requirements rather than simply following the shortest available path. Power and Ground Power distribution networks are designed to provide stable and low-impedance power delivery. Ground planes are carefully maintained to provide appropriate return paths and reduce unwanted noise and electromagnetic interference. General Signals After critical nets have been addressed, general signal routing is completed according to the defined design rules for: Trace width Trace spacing Via size Clearance Routing layers Manufacturing limitations For dense boards, routing may require multiple iterations of placement and routing optimization to achieve a balance between electrical performance and manufacturability. Step 5– Layout Optimization and Verification After routing is completed, the PCB layout undergoes a detailed optimization and verification process. This stage may include: Copper Pour and Plane Optimization Copper pours and power/ground planes are optimized to improve current return paths, grounding, shielding, and thermal performance. Silkscreen Optimization Reference designators, polarity markings, pin-1 indicators, and other assembly information are adjusted to improve readability and prevent interference with pads or other components. Design Rule Check (DRC) Automated DRC is performed to identify potential violations such as: Clearance violations Trace width violations Unconnected nets Via and drill violations Component spacing issues Copper-to-board-edge violations Other manufacturer-specific rule violations Engineer Review Beyond automated DRC, the layout is also reviewed from an engineering perspective. Depending on the project, this may include checking: Signal integrity Power integrity Thermal performance EMI/EMC considerations High-speed routing Manufacturing constraints Assembly requirements Mechanical compatibility Automated checks can identify rule violations, but they cannot replace engineering judgment. A professional PCB review therefore combines software-based verification with engineering inspection. Step 6 – Design Review and Customer Approval Before generating final manufacturing data, the completed PCB layout is provided to the customer for review. The customer can verify key aspects of the design, including: Component locations Board dimensions Connector positions Mechanical interfaces Silkscreen information Routing and design intent Any required changes are incorporated before the design is released for manufacturing. This review stage provides an important checkpoint between PCB design and production and helps ensure that the final layout accurately reflects the customer's design requirements. Step 7 – Manufacturing Data Generation Once the PCB layout has been approved, the final manufacturing data is generated. Depending on the project, the manufacturing package may include: Gerber files NC drill files PCB fabrication drawings Bill of Materials (BOM) Pick-and-place files Assembly drawings Stack-up information Other manufacturing documentation Gerber files contain the graphical information required to manufacture the PCB, including copper layers, solder mask, silkscreen, and other fabrication layers. For PCB assembly projects, the BOM and pick-and-place files provide the component and placement information required for SMT assembly. Before release, the output files are checked to ensure that the generated manufacturing data is consistent with the approved PCB design. Step 8 – DFM and PCB Manufacturing The final stage is transferring the verified manufacturing data into production. Before fabrication, the manufacturing data can be evaluated against the PCB manufacturer's capabilities through Design for Manufacturability (DFM) checks. Typical DFM considerations include: Minimum trace width and spacing Minimum drill size Copper-to-edge clearance Annular ring requirements Solder mask clearance Via structures Board thickness Copper thickness Surface finish Manufacturing tolerances Manufacturing requirements are considered from the very beginning of PCBWay's PCB layout process, helping minimize production issues and unnecessary manufacturing delays. What’s more, upon completion of the PCB Layout order, free technical support and a permanent 5% discount on PCBA production will be provided. Why Professional PCB Layout Matters PCB layout has a direct impact on the performance and manufacturability of an electronic product. A professional PCB layout should consider the entire product development process—not just whether all components are electrically connected. Depending on the application, the layout may need to address: Signal Integrity (SI) Power Integrity (PI) EMI/EMC Thermal Management High-Speed Design Design for Manufacturability (DFM) Design for Assembly (DFA) Mechanical Integration Reliability and Serviceability The earlier these factors are considered, the fewer problems are likely to appear during prototype validation and mass production. At PCBWay, our PCB design engineers work with customers throughout the layout process, helping transform circuit concepts and schematics into manufacturable, reliable, and production-ready PCB designs. If you are looking for professional PCB layout or PCB design services, feel free to contact us or submit PCB Layout requirement here. Our engineering team can help evaluate your design and develop a PCB layout optimized for both performance and manufacturing.
